technical.prompt: Who are the main lenders to commercial real estate?

choices.answer: Banks, insurers, CMBS conduits, debt funds and housing agencies
distractors: Only central banks and governments
Only tenants who occupy the buildings
Only the property's original developer

technical.prompt: What is a bridge loan in real estate?
expectedPoints: Used for properties in transition, such as lease-up or renovation
Refinanced with permanent debt once stabilised

choices.answer: Short-term financing for a property in transition until it stabilises
distractors: A long-term fixed loan on a fully leased building
A loan used to build bridges and roads
A loan from one tenant to another

technical.prompt: What is a permanent loan?
expectedPoints: Longer-term financing on a stabilised property

choices.answer: Longer-term, often fixed-rate financing on a stabilised property
distractors: A loan that never has to be repaid
A short loan used during construction
A loan secured on the owner's home

technical.prompt: What is yield maintenance?
expectedPoints: A prepayment penalty that compensates the lender for lost interest
Based on the gap between the loan rate and current market rates
Larger when market rates have fallen

choices.answer: A prepayment penalty compensating the lender for lost interest
distractors: A fee to keep a property's rental yield steady
A reserve for building maintenance
A rule that rent must rise every year

technical.prompt: What is defeasance?
expectedPoints: Replacing a loan's collateral with government securities
The securities cover the remaining payments
Lets the property be sold or refinanced

choices.answer: Swapping the collateral for government securities that cover the payments
distractors: Cancelling the loan entirely after a borrower's default
Reducing the loan's interest rate by mutual agreement
Transferring the loan to a new borrower without consent

technical.prompt: What is a cash trap in a property loan?
expectedPoints: Excess cash is held by the lender instead of going to the owner
Triggered when performance falls below a threshold
Such as a debt service coverage test

choices.answer: Excess cash held back from the owner when performance weakens
distractors: A penalty for paying the loan early
A safe for storing rent payments
A fee charged for each late payment

technical.prompt: What reserves do lenders often require on property loans?
expectedPoints: Leasing reserves for tenant improvements and commissions

choices.answer: Tax, insurance, repair, leasing and sometimes interest reserves
distractors: Only a reserve for the owner's salary
Only a reserve for marketing costs
Only a reserve for future acquisitions

technical.prompt: What are extension options on a property loan?
expectedPoints: The borrower can extend maturity for set periods

choices.answer: The right to extend maturity if certain tests are met
distractors: The lender's right to demand early repayment
A clause that lowers the interest rate each year
A promise to lend more money later

technical.prompt: What is mezzanine debt in real estate?
expectedPoints: Debt sitting between the mortgage and equity
Secured by a pledge of the ownership interests
Foreclosure is on the equity interests

choices.answer: Debt between the mortgage and equity, secured by ownership interests
distractors: The senior mortgage that is secured on the building itself
A loan made to a tenant to pay for its office fit-out
Equity held by the company that manages the property

technical.prompt: What is an A/B note structure?
expectedPoints: A mortgage split into a senior A note and a junior B note
Lets lenders sell pieces to different investors

choices.answer: A mortgage split into senior and junior pieces on the same collateral
distractors: Two separate loans secured on two different buildings
A single loan repaid in two different currencies
A loan shared between two unrelated borrowers

technical.prompt: What is special servicing for a CMBS loan?
expectedPoints: A special servicer takes over when a loan is in trouble

choices.answer: Handling of troubled CMBS loans by a dedicated servicer
distractors: Premium customer service for tenants
A servicer that collects only on-time payments
A lender that services only luxury buildings

technical.prompt: What is the difference between as-is and as-stabilised value?
expectedPoints: As-is: value today in current condition
As-stabilised: value after the business plan is complete

choices.answer: Value today versus value after the business plan is complete
distractors: Value before tax versus after tax
Value of land versus buildings
Value in one city versus another

technical.prompt: What is future funding in a bridge loan?
expectedPoints: Loan amounts released later for capex or leasing
Aligns funding with the business plan

choices.answer: Loan money released later for capex or leasing as milestones are met
distractors: Funding promised from a future sale
Interest that is paid in the future
Money lent to buy future properties

technical.prompt: How is a commercial real estate loan typically priced?
expectedPoints: Spread over a benchmark rate or fixed coupon
Depends on leverage and property risk

choices.answer: A spread or fixed rate plus fees, set by leverage and risk
distractors: A share of the property's rent
A percentage of the tenant's profit
A fixed fee with no interest

technical.prompt: What is the difference between a recourse and a non-recourse property loan?
expectedPoints: Recourse: lender can pursue the borrower's other assets
Non-recourse: lender is limited to the property
Recourse loans may be priced lower

choices.answer: Recourse reaches other assets; non-recourse is limited to the property
distractors: Non-recourse lets the lender seize any asset the borrower owns
Recourse loans are made without any collateral at all
The two types differ only in their interest rates

technical.prompt: What is a deed in lieu of foreclosure?
expectedPoints: Borrower hands the property to the lender voluntarily

choices.answer: The borrower voluntarily hands the property to the lender
distractors: The lender forgives the loan entirely
The borrower buys the lender's business
A new tenant takes over the lease

technical.prompt: What is a CRE CLO?
expectedPoints: A securitisation of commercial real estate loans, often bridge loans

choices.answer: A securitisation of commercial property loans, often bridge loans
distractors: A single large loan made to one property owner
A fund that buys shares in listed property companies
A government programme that builds public housing

technical.prompt: Why do lenders assess the sponsor as well as the property?

choices.answer: The sponsor's skill and strength decide if the plan and loan succeed
distractors: Sponsors personally pay the tenants' rent each month
Sponsors guarantee that property values will rise
Sponsors set the interest rate charged on the loan

technical.prompt: What is the difference between a term default and a maturity default?
expectedPoints: Term default: missing payments or breaking covenants during the loan
Maturity default: failing to repay at maturity
Maturity defaults often come from refinancing problems

choices.answer: Term default occurs during the loan; maturity default is not repaying at the end
distractors: Term default occurs at the end; maturity default happens during the loan
The two terms describe exactly the same event
Neither type of default involves any missed payment

technical.prompt: A $20 million loan has a 6% coupon and three years left, paying interest annually. Market rates have fallen to 4%. If yield maintenance equals the lost interest discounted at the 4% market rate, roughly what penalty would apply?
expectedPoints: Present value over 3 years at 4%: about $0.4M x 2.78

choices.answer: About $1.1 million
distractors: About $1.2 million
About $0.4 million
About $2.4 million

technical.prompt: A loan traps excess cash if debt service coverage falls below 1.10x. Why would a lender include this?
expectedPoints: Builds a cushion when performance weakens
Stops cash leaking to the owner
Cash can be released if performance recovers

choices.answer: To build a cushion and stop cash leaving as performance weakens
distractors: To reward the owner for especially strong performance
To pay the lender's own servicing and legal fees
To reduce the interest rate charged on the loan

technical.prompt: A bridge lender funds 70% of total project cost, which is a $25 million purchase plus $5 million of renovations. The stabilised value is expected to be $40 million. What is the loan and its stabilised loan-to-value?

choices.answer: $21 million; 52.5% of stabilised value
distractors: $28 million; 70% of stabilised value
$21 million; 70% of stabilised value
$17.5 million; 43.75% of stabilised value

distractors: Passes; no paydown needed

technical.prompt: A floating loan pays the benchmark rate of 5% plus 3%, with a 1% origination fee on an expected two-year life. What is the approximate all-in yield?

choices.answer: About 8.5%
distractors: About 8.2%

technical.prompt: Where do a mezzanine loan's attachment and detachment points sit if the senior loan is 60% loan-to-value and total debt is 75%?
expectedPoints: Mezzanine loses money once value falls below 75% of original
Wiped out if value falls below 60%

choices.answer: Attaches at 60% and detaches at 75%
distractors: Attaches at 0% and detaches at 60%
Attaches at 75% and detaches at 100%
Attaches at 15% and detaches at 75%

technical.prompt: How does defeasance differ from yield maintenance for the borrower?
expectedPoints: Defeasance: buy government securities to replace the collateral
Yield maintenance: pay a cash penalty
Both costlier when rates have fallen
Defeasance keeps the loan outstanding in the securitisation

choices.answer: Defeasance swaps in securities; yield maintenance is a cash penalty
distractors: Defeasance cancels the debt; yield maintenance raises the rent
Both become free for the borrower when rates fall
Yield maintenance swaps in securities as collateral

technical.prompt: How do banks, insurers and debt funds differ as real estate lenders?
expectedPoints: Banks: relationship lending, often recourse or shorter terms
Insurers: long fixed-rate loans on high-quality assets

technical.prompt: Why do lenders often size bridge loans on both as-is and as-stabilised values?

distractors: Regulators require exactly two appraisals for every loan

distractors: CMBS loans can't default
